metaData.title: 6IT
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a detailed, bottom-up explanation of CPU physics and memory hierarchy, from register operations and cache latencies to main memory and network access times, with practical advice for C++ developers.
metaData.summary: This is the draft of a chapter from a forthcoming book on efficient C++ programming for modern 64-bit CPUs. It begins with the fundamental principle that physical distance correlates with access latency, driven by parasitic capacitance. The article then systematically explores the memory hierarchy: core-level operations (register-register, ALU, L1/L2 cache latencies), chip-level (L3 cache, main memory), motherboard-level (RAM, NVMe/SSD/HDD latencies, fsync costs), and the outside world (LAN, Wi-Fi, ISP, inter-city network latencies). It includes detailed discussions on branch mispredictions and the `[[likely]]`/`[[unlikely]]` attributes, TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) and its impact on vector vs. node-based data structures, and a C/C++ perspective on memory storage (stack, static, heap, thread-local). The article is rich with specific cycle-time numbers and references to authoritative sources like Agner Fog and Denis Bakhvalov.

mainPoints.point: Physical distance is the primary driver of memory access latency in modern CPUs.
mainPoints.explanation: The article explains that parasitic capacitances, which are proportional to connection length, govern signal speeds. This principle applies from on-chip caches to network cables, with latencies increasing by orders of magnitude at each level.

mainPoints.point: Modern superscalar CPUs can retire multiple instructions per cycle, but achieving high RIPC is challenging.
mainPoints.explanation: While CPUs can theoretically achieve 10-12 Retired Instructions Per Cycle (RIPC), in practice, achieving even 4 is difficult and is usually limited to ALU-bound algorithms, not RAM-bound ones.

mainPoints.point: The `[[likely]]`/`[[unlikely]]` attributes have limited effectiveness due to dynamic branch prediction.
mainPoints.explanation: Modern CPUs use runtime statistics for branch prediction. These attributes only help for totally new branch instructions, which are rare. The authors recommend using them only when you are 'at least 200% sure' the branch is very unlikely, such as for error handling.

mainPoints.point: For de-pessimized C++ programs using vectors, DTLB misses are less of a concern than for C-style node-based programs.
mainPoints.explanation: Linear data structures like `std::vector` minimize pressure on the Data TLB (DTLB). The authors note that TLB issues are more relevant for apps using enormous amounts of RAM (databases, JVM) or in virtualized environments, and can often be mitigated with huge pages.

mainPoints.point: Heap data should be considered uncached unless accessing recently accessed or linearly scanned memory.
mainPoints.explanation: Unlike stack data, which is almost guaranteed to be cached, heap data caching is unreliable. The article emphasizes that linear scans of `std::vector` benefit from caching, but operations like `binary_search` over large vectors do not.

keyQuotes: the farther physically our electrical signal has to go, the slower our access is.
characteristic times of electronic signals are restricted by so-called parasitic capacitances, and parasitic capacitances in general are proportional to the length of the connection
we would *not* recommend using `[[likely]]`/`[[unlikely]]` attributes, *unless you are at least 200% sure that the branch is indeed very unlikely*.

for a de-pessimized C++ program relying mostly on vectors, we expect effects related to DTLB misses to be observably smaller to that of the programs written in C-style and relying on node-based data structures
heap data should be considered as uncached (sic!) -- that is, unless we *know* that we recently accessed something nearby

relatedArticles.title: How OpenAI delivers low-latency voice AI at scale
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI rearchitected its WebRTC stack using a split relay and transceiver model to deliver low-latency voice AI at scale, solving port exhaustion and state stickiness in Kubernetes.

relatedArticles.title: Fast regex search: indexing text for agent tools
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cursor explains the evolution of regex indexing and their implementation of a local, frequency-weighted sparse n-gram index to accelerate AI agent searches in large monorepos.

relatedArticles.title: Software Architecture Guide
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This page from Martin Fowler presents his perspective on software architecture, defining it as the important stuff in system design, and serves as a curated guide to his site's extensive resources on application and enterprise architecture.

relatedArticles.title: State of the Claw
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenClaw founder and OpenAI engineer Peter Steinberger discusses the unprecedented growth and security challenges of the OpenClaw project, shares his unique AI-assisted development workflow, and explores the evolving concept of 'engineer taste' in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineers detail a five-month experiment building a production software product with zero manually-written code, using Codex agents to achieve 10x velocity and redefining the engineer's role as system designer and feedback loop architect.

relatedArticles.title: Lessons from building Claude Code: Prompt caching is everything | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the critical, often unintuitive, lessons learned from optimizing prompt caching in Claude Code, emphasizing that designing an agent's entire architecture around prefix-matching caching is essential for performance and cost.

relatedArticles.title: Xiaomi MiMo， Explore and Love
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Xiaomi MiMo and TileRT achieve 1000+ tokens/s inference on a 1-trillion-parameter model using commodity GPUs through extreme model-system codesign, including FP4 quantization and DFlash speculative decoding.

relatedArticles.title: Dario Amodei — Policy on the AI Exponential
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Dario Amodei argues that AI is advancing exponentially, creating a dangerous mismatch with slow-moving policy, and proposes concrete actions across regulation, economics, science, civil liberties, and geopolitics to meet the moment.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering: How to Build Software When Humans Steer, Agents Execute
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineer Ryan Lopopolo introduces 'Harness Engineering,' a paradigm shift where engineers design systems and automated guardrails to orchestrate hundreds of AI agents, transforming from coders to directors of software development.

relatedArticles.title: Inside FAISS: Billion-Scale Similarity Search
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep, visual, and intuitive explanation of FAISS, covering the core ideas of IVF, Product Quantization, their combination in IVFPQ, and GPU acceleration, to enable billion-scale similarity search.
